reason: Introduces the basic set‑up: a universal square‑free polynomial and its root cover πₙ → Uₙ.  The Chebotarev density theorem for the Sₙ‑monodromy yields the harmonic number Lₙ, the same technique needed for the conic‑tangency cover.

Adds a square‑root of the discriminant, yielding a degree‑2 étale extension of the universal cover.  It shows how extra étale data (as in the discriminant condition for tangency) does not change the harmonic‑number computation.

Studies the ordered‑pair cover Y → Uₙ of distinct roots, whose fibre has degree n(n‑1).  The problem uses the fixed‑point statistic X(σ)(X(σ)‑1) and the moment formulas for a random permutation, a prototype for the more intricate tangency condition.

Provides a concrete geometric incidence problem (smooth conic ↔ smooth cubic) whose fibre parametrises cubic curves meeting a fixed conic.  The monodromy is S₆ and the average number of components is obtained via Chebotarev, mirroring the set‑up of Z → U⁵.

Reformulates a tangency‑type condition algebraically: the unordered pair of distinct roots of a quartic.  Its fibre has degree 6 and monodromy S₆, illustrating how a geometric contact condition can be encoded by a discriminant‑square hypothesis.

Treats a higher‑dimensional enumerative problem (lines meeting six skew lines) with fibre of degree 12 and monodromy S₁₂.  The analysis of connected components via Frobenius cycles is formally identical to the conic‑tangency situation and prepares the student for dealing with large symmetric‑group monodromy.

Shows how imposing a square‑discriminant condition forces the geometric monodromy to the alternating group A₇.  Understanding this reduction is essential for recognizing why the conic‑tangency cover, despite its discriminant constraints, still has full symmetric monodromy.

Gives a case where the monodromy group is a proper simple subgroup PSL₂(𝔽₇)⊂S₇.  The computation of the average number of components via the class‑by‑class count teaches the student to verify that the conic‑tangency problem really has full S_{3264} and not a smaller subgroup.

Analyzes the ordered‑root scheme Zₙ → Uₙ with fibre n! and monodromy S_{n!}.  The number of connected components equals the number of cycles of the Frobenius action on orderings, exactly the combinatorial object that appears when counting the 3264 conics tangent to five given conics.

States the general theorem that the average number of irreducible factors of a square‑free degree‑n polynomial equals the n‑th harmonic number Hₙ, and asks for n = 3264.  Computing ⌊100·H₃₂₆₄⌋ reproduces the final numeric answer required for the conic‑tangency problem, tying together all previous monodromy and Chebotarev arguments.

Computes the limit of the average number of fixed points of a random permutation acting on a finite set; this is the combinatorial model for the Chebotarev argument that the average fibre size of a finite étale cover equals the number of orbits of its geometric monodromy.

Classical Schubert problem of lines meeting four general lines in ℙ³; the incidence variety is a degree‑2 finite étale cover of an open subset, and one proves that the average number of rational lines tends to 1, mirroring the conic‑tangency situation for five conics.

Studies monic degree‑5 polynomials with full S₅ Galois group; averaging the number of ℱₚ‑rational roots uses the same Sₙ‑monodromy/average‑fixed‑point principle that appears for the 3264 tangent‑conic cover.

Considers the zero‑dimensional scheme cut out by a quadratic and a cubic in ℝ², giving a degree‑6 étale cover of the a‑line; the computation of L uses Bézout, smoothness, and the expectation of fixed points of a random element of S₆.

Counts ℱₚ‑rational common tangent lines to four smooth plane conics; the incidence correspondence is analogous to the one for conics tangent to five conics, and the same monodromy‑symmetry ideas give the average count needed for the target problem.

Intersection of a quadric, two cubics and a quartic in ℙ³ produces a zero‑dimensional scheme of degree 2·3·3·4; analysing its average number of ℱₚ‑points introduces genericity, Bézout, and the passage from geometric degree to arithmetic averages.

Average number of ℱₚ‑points of the complete intersection of five random quadrics in ℙ⁵; this higher‑dimensional analogue of the conic‑tangency incidence variety illustrates how to set up the counting problem in a parameter space of quadrics.

Same computation as 91 but in ℙ³, giving a concrete model where the ambient space has the same dimension as the plane of conics (ℙ⁵) after projectivising the space of conics; it reinforces the use of generic complete intersections and Lang–Weil estimates.

Averaging point counts on the fibres of the elliptic surface y² = x³ + t over ℱₚ; the argument uses Hasse–Weil bounds and the fact that the fibrewise point count is p + 1 on average, a prototype for the limit definition of L in the conic‑tangency problem.

Gives the exact expected number of cycles of a random even permutation (alternating group); the parity restriction mimics the double‑cover defined by the discriminant hypersurface in the space of smooth conics, helping the learner understand how symmetry constraints affect average counts.
